deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics by Gauss. It is page xv of the printed historical preface to a German textbook of arithmetic and algebra. The bundle name suggests Christian Leiste's 'Die Arithmetic und Algebra' (Wolfenbüttel, 1790), which Gauss used as a schoolboy. The only manuscript traces are three small hand marks: the word 'Schon' is underlined, a '2' is written in the right margin beside the line '† 1728) die erste Veranlassung zu seinen großen Entdeckun=', and there is a small asterisk-like mark just below it. They may be Gauss's, but that is unverifiable from the image.

The printed text continues a historical survey of algebra from the previous page. In order, it covers the following.

(4) John Wallis, continued:
- Pelshover of Königsberg witnessed a sample of Wallis's mental extraction of square roots in 1670.
- Wallis was a Doctor of Theology and a leading founding member of the Royal Society.
- His Opera mathematica in three folio volumes appeared at Oxford (dates printed as 1663, 65, 99).
- He first used negative exponents for fractions, i.e. x^(-n) = 1/x^n (cross-reference to the book's §51).
- He studied the sums of squares and cubes (§153), presumably the formulas sum k^2 = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 and sum k^3 = (n(n+1)/2)^2, and the calculus of the infinite (Arithmetica infinitorum).
- Together with Barrow, he gave Newton the first impulse to his discoveries.

(5) Isaac Newton (printed 'geb. 1642 † 1728'):
- His series for the circle, from interpolating Wallis's quadratures of (1-x^2)^(n/2), led him to the general binomial series (§104). The text notes this is also ascribed to Pascal, meaning the arithmetic triangle for integer exponents.
- He taught the use of fractional exponents.
- He invented 'the method of §188' and other devices for finding the roots of equations. This is probably Newton's method of approximation, or his method of divisors; it is unclear without the book.
- He gave a rule for the number of imaginary roots of higher equations, which Maclaurin and Campbell later treated better.
- At age 27 he is said to have communicated the foundations of fluxions to Barrow. From this, together with Leibniz's independent invention, the differential and integral calculus arose.

(6) Leibniz:
- Born 1646 in Leipzig.
- Promoted learning through his own work and through founding academies.
- Reached the calculus of the infinite through higher geometry.
- Engaged in the priority dispute with Newton; the verdict in Newton's favour is alleged to have hastened his death in 1716.
- The page ends with the remark that the English first learned the calculus not from Newton himself (continued on the next page).

There are no derivations to reconstruct. Implicit formulas are supplied in CHECKABLE as my own glosses.
errors: Newton's death is printed as 1728. He died 20 March 1726/7 (Old Style), i.e. 31 March 1727 (New Style).
Wallis's Opera mathematica appeared at Oxford in 1693, 1695 and 1699, not '1663, 65 und 99'. The first two dates are off by 30 years, probably a misprint.

Calling Wallis the first to use negative exponents is the conventional 18th-century attribution. Nicole Oresme, Nicolas Chuquet and Michael Stifel had related notations earlier, though Wallis (Arithmetica infinitorum, 1656) first used them systematically.

Ascribing the binomial theorem to Pascal is loose. Pascal (Traité du triangle arithmétique, written c. 1654, published 1665) treated only positive integer exponents. The general series for arbitrary exponents is Newton's (1664/65, communicated in the Epistola prior of 1676).
Saying Newton 'taught the use of fractional exponents' overlooks Wallis's earlier use of fractional indices; Newton adopted and generalized the notation.

Newton's rule for the number of imaginary roots (Arithmetica universalis, 1707) was stated without proof; Maclaurin and George Campbell (1728) gave partial demonstrations. A full proof came only from Sylvester (1865), so 'better than Newton' is fair but incomplete.

Newton's rule for counting imaginary roots
Newton-Leibniz invention of the calculus and priority dispute

deep.surprise_reason: This is a printed page of historical narrative from a school textbook (Leiste) owned and used by Gauss. It contains no Gaussian mathematics; the only hand traces are an underline, a marginal '2' and a small mark.

transcription_corrections: The machine transcription is essentially accurate. 'Krais' (for Kreis) and 'Leibnitz' are the original spellings, not errors.

Hand annotations: the word 'Schon' is underlined in ink. The marginal '2' sits beside the line '† 1728) die erste Veranlassung zu seinen großen Entdeckun=', with a small asterisk/cross-like mark just below it, near 'gen. Durch seine Reihe für den Krais'.
The page number is 'xv' in lower-case roman, as printed.
